text: A Neural Network is a machine learning algorithm inspired by the way biological neurons process information. Neural networks are particularly powerful because they can learn complex and non-linear relationships from data. They are widely used in: Image classification Object detection Natural Language Processing (NLP) Speech recognition Recommendation systems Fraud detection Time-series prediction Generative AI A neural network learns by adjusting numerical parameters called weights and biases during training.

metadata.section: Document 1: Neural Networks in Machine Learning > 1. Introduction

text: A neural network is usually composed of three types of layers: Input Layer → Hidden Layer(s) → Output Layer

metadata.section: Document 1: Neural Networks in Machine Learning > 2. Basic Structure of a Neural Network

text: The input layer receives the features of the dataset. For example, if we want to predict house prices: Features: - House size - Number of bedrooms - Location - Age of house These features become the inputs to the neural network.

metadata.section: Document 1: Neural Networks in Machine Learning > 2. Basic Structure of a Neural Network > Input Layer

text: Hidden layers perform transformations on the input data. A neural network can have: One hidden layer Several hidden layers Hundreds of layers in very deep networks When a network has many layers, we commonly call it a Deep Neural Network (DNN).

metadata.section: Document 1: Neural Networks in Machine Learning > 2. Basic Structure of a Neural Network > Hidden Layers

text: The output layer produces the final prediction. For example: Binary classification Customer → Neural Network → Probability of Churn → 0.87 The model might interpret 0.87 as an 87% probability that the customer will churn.

metadata.section: Document 1: Neural Networks in Machine Learning > 2. Basic Structure of a Neural Network > Output Layer

text: The fundamental building block of a neural network is the neuron. A neuron receives several inputs. For example: x₁ ──→ \ x₂ ───→ Neuron ──→ Output / x₃ ──→ Each input has an associated weight. The neuron calculates: z=w1 x1 +w2 x2 +...+wn xn +b Where: x = input w = weight b = bias z = weighted sum The result is then passed through an activation function: a=f(z)

metadata.section: 3. What Is a Neuron?

text: Weights determine the importance of each feature. For example, suppose we are predicting whether a student will pass an exam. Study Hours → weight = 0.8 Attendance → weight = 0.5 Previous Grade → weight = 0.3 A larger weight means that the model considers that feature more influential in its current representation. During training, the neural network learns appropriate weights automatically.

metadata.section: 4. Why Do We Need Weights?

text: The bias allows the neuron to shift its activation. The basic equation becomes: z=wx+b Without a bias, the model has less flexibility. Bias is therefore another parameter learned during training.

metadata.section: 5. Bias

text: Activation functions introduce non-linearity into the neural network. Without activation functions, stacking many layers would still result in essentially a linear transformation. Common activation functions include:

metadata.section: 6. Activation Functions

text: ReLU(x)=max(0,x) Example: x = -5 → 0 x = 3 → 3 ReLU is commonly used in hidden layers.

metadata.section: 6. Activation Functions > ReLU

text: σ(x)=1+e−x1 It produces values between: 0 and 1 It is commonly used for binary classification output.

metadata.section: 6. Activation Functions > ReLU > Sigmoid

text: Softmax converts multiple output scores into probabilities. For example: Cat → 0.70 Dog → 0.20 Horse → 0.10 The probabilities sum to 1. Softmax is commonly used for multi-class classification.

metadata.section: 6. Activation Functions > ReLU > Softmax

text: Forward propagation is the process of sending data through the network to produce a prediction. Example: Input ↓ Layer 1 ↓ Layer 2 ↓ Layer 3 ↓ Output At each layer: Inputs are multiplied by weights. Bias is added. Activation function is applied. The result is passed to the next layer. Eventually, the network produces a prediction.

metadata.section: 7. Forward Propagation

text: The model needs a way to measure whether its prediction is good or bad. This is the job of the loss function. Example: Actual value: 1 Predicted value: 0.8 The loss function calculates how far the prediction is from the target. Common loss functions include:

metadata.section: 8. Loss Function

text: Usually used for regression: MSE=n1 ∑(y−y^ )2

metadata.section: 8. Loss Function > Mean Squared Error

text: Commonly used for classification. The objective of training is: Minimize Loss

metadata.section: 8. Loss Function > Mean Squared Error > Cross-Entropy Loss

text: After calculating the loss, the network needs to determine: Which weights caused the error? This is done using backpropagation. The algorithm calculates gradients of the loss with respect to the model's parameters. Conceptually: Prediction ↓ Calculate Loss ↓ Backpropagation ↓ Calculate Gradients ↓ Update Weights

metadata.section: 9. Backpropagation

text: The gradients tell the optimizer how to modify the parameters. A simplified update equation is: wnew =wold −η∂w∂L Where: w = weight L = loss η = learning rate The learning rate controls how large each update is. If the learning rate is:

metadata.section: 10. Gradient Descent > Too large

text: Training a neural network generally follows this process: Training Data ↓ Forward Propagation ↓ Prediction ↓ Calculate Loss ↓ Backpropagation ↓ Calculate Gradients ↓ Optimizer ↓ Update Weights ↓ Repeat This process is repeated many times. One complete pass through the training dataset is called an epoch.

text: Clustering is an unsupervised machine learning technique used to discover groups or structures within data. Unlike supervised learning, clustering does not require labeled examples. For example, suppose we have customer data: Customer A Customer B Customer C Customer D Customer E We don't know the customer categories beforehand. A clustering algorithm might discover: Cluster 1 → High-value customers Cluster 2 → Occasional customers Cluster 3 → Low-value customers The algorithm discovers these groups from the data.

metadata.section: 1. Introduction

text: We have: Input → Known Label Example: Email → Spam Email → Not Spam The model learns from known labels.

metadata.section: 2. Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning > Supervised Learning

text: We have: Input → No Label The algorithm tries to discover structure. Customer Data ↓ Clustering ↓ Discovered Groups

metadata.section: 2. Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning > Supervised Learning > Unsupervised Learning

text: A cluster is a group of data points that are considered similar according to some measure. For example: ● ● ● ● ● ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ■ ■ ■ ■ We might discover three clusters: Cluster 1 → ● Cluster 2 → ▲ Cluster 3 → ■ The definition of "similar" depends on the algorithm.

metadata.section: 3. What Is a Cluster?

text: Many clustering algorithms depend on measuring distance. A common measure is Euclidean distance. For two points: A=(x1 ,y1 ) and B=(x2 ,y2 ) the distance is: d(A,B)=(x2 −x1 )2+(y2 −y1 )2 Other similarity or distance measures include: Manhattan distance Cosine similarity Euclidean distance Mahalanobis distance

metadata.section: 4. Distance Measures

text: K-Means is one of the most popular clustering algorithms. The user must specify: K = Number of clusters For example: K = 3 means that we want three clusters.

metadata.section: 5. K-Means Clustering

text: Suppose we have data points and want: K = 3

metadata.section: 6. How K-Means Works

text: The algorithm selects three initial centroids. Centroid 1 Centroid 2 Centroid 3

metadata.section: 6. How K-Means Works > Step 1: Initialize Centroids

text: Each data point is assigned to its nearest centroid. Point → Nearest Centroid

metadata.section: 6. How K-Means Works > Step 1: Initialize Centroids > Step 2: Assign Points

text: For each cluster, calculate the mean position of all points. New Centroid = Mean of cluster points

metadata.section: 6. How K-Means Works > Step 1: Initialize Centroids > Step 3: Recalculate Centroids

text: Repeat: Assign → Recalculate → Assign → Recalculate until the centroids stop changing significantly.

metadata.section: 6. How K-Means Works > Step 1: Initialize Centroids > Step 4: Repeat

text: Imagine customers described by: Annual Spending Purchase Frequency The data might look like: Spending ↑ | | ● ● ● | | ▲ ▲ | | ■ ■ ■ +--------------------→ Frequency K-Means could discover: Cluster 1 → Low spending Cluster 2 → Medium spending Cluster 3 → High spending

metadata.section: 7. K-Means Example

text: K-Means attempts to minimize the distance between points and their assigned centroid. This is commonly expressed as minimizing the within-cluster sum of squares: i=1∑K x∈Ci ∑ ∣∣x−μi ∣∣2 Where: K = number of clusters Ci = cluster x = data point μi = cluster centroid

metadata.section: 8. K-Means Objective

text: One of the biggest questions in K-Means is: How do we choose K? Two common approaches are:

metadata.section: 9. Choosing K

text: Run K-Means with different values of K. For example: K = 2 K = 3 K = 4 K = 5 K = 6 Calculate the clustering error for each value. Usually, the error decreases as K increases. We look for an elbow point, where increasing K provides significantly less improvement.

metadata.section: 9. Choosing K > Elbow Method

text: The Silhouette Score evaluates how well a point fits within its cluster. The score generally ranges from: -1 to +1 Interpretation: Close to +1 → Good clustering Around 0 → Overlapping clusters Below 0 → Potentially incorrect assignments A higher score generally indicates better-separated clusters.

metadata.section: 10. Silhouette Score

text: Hierarchical clustering creates a hierarchy of clusters. One common approach is Agglomerative Clustering. It starts with every point as its own cluster: A B C D E Then it repeatedly merges the closest clusters: AB C D E AB CD E ABCD E ABCDE The result can be represented using a dendrogram.

metadata.section: 11. Hierarchical Clustering

text: A dendrogram is a tree-like visualization showing how clusters are merged. Conceptually: ┌───────────────┐ │ │ ┌─┴─┐ ┌─┴─┐ A B C D We can cut the dendrogram at a certain level to determine the number of clusters.

metadata.section: 12. Dendrogram

text: DBSCAN stands for: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise Unlike K-Means, DBSCAN does not require us to specify K. Instead, it works based on density. It can identify: Dense regions Sparse regions Noise Irregularly shaped clusters

metadata.section: 13. DBSCAN

text: Two important parameters are:

metadata.section: 14. DBSCAN Parameters

text: The radius used to define a neighborhood.

metadata.section: 14. DBSCAN Parameters > eps

text: The minimum number of nearby points required to consider an area sufficiently dense. Conceptually: Dense region ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● Sparse region ● ● DBSCAN can identify the dense area as a cluster and potentially classify isolated points as noise.

metadata.section: 14. DBSCAN Parameters > eps > min_samples

text: Consider this dataset: ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ ▲ The clusters have irregular shapes. K-Means may struggle because it tends to create clusters around centroids. DBSCAN can handle many irregular shapes because it focuses on density.

metadata.section: 15. Why DBSCAN Is Useful

text: A Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) assumes that the data comes from a mixture of several Gaussian probability distributions. Instead of saying: Point X → Cluster 1 GMM can say: Point X: Cluster 1 → 80% Cluster 2 → 20% This is called soft clustering. K-Means generally performs hard assignments: Point → Cluster 1

metadata.section: 16. Gaussian Mixture Models

text: Each point belongs to one cluster. Customer A → Cluster 1 Customer B → Cluster 2 Customer C → Cluster 1 K-Means is an example.

metadata.section: 17. Hard vs Soft Clustering > Hard Clustering

text: A point can have probabilities for multiple clusters. Customer A: Cluster 1 → 70% Cluster 2 → 30% GMM is an example.

metadata.section: 17. Hard vs Soft Clustering > Hard Clustering > Soft Clustering

metadata.section: 19. Data Preprocessing for Clustering

text: Missing values can affect distance calculations. Possible solutions: Remove rows OR Impute missing values

metadata.section: 19. Data Preprocessing for Clustering > Handle Missing Values

text: Suppose we have: Age: 20–80 Salary: 10,000–500,000 Salary has a much larger numerical scale. Distance-based algorithms may therefore give salary disproportionate influence. We can use: Standardization Min-Max Scaling For example: z=σx−μ

metadata.section: 19. Data Preprocessing for Clustering > Handle Missing Values > Feature Scaling

text: Outliers can strongly affect some clustering algorithms. Example: ● ● ● ● ● ● ● X The X could be an unusual observation. Depending on the problem, we may: Investigate the outlier Remove it Transform the data Use an algorithm such as DBSCAN that can identify noise

text: Suppose an e-commerce company has: Customer ID Annual Spending Purchase Frequency Average Order Value We can use clustering to discover customer groups. Example: Cluster 1 High spending High frequency Cluster 2 Medium spending Medium frequency Cluster 3 Low spending Low frequency The business can then create different strategies for each segment. For example: Cluster 1 → VIP rewards Cluster 2 → Personalized promotions Cluster 3 → Discount campaigns

text: Clustering does not automatically tell us what a cluster means. For example, the algorithm may produce: Cluster 1 Cluster 2 Cluster 3 It does not automatically know: Cluster 1 = VIP customers Cluster 2 = Normal customers Cluster 3 = Inactive customers Humans or downstream analysis must interpret the clusters. Other limitations include: Choosing the correct algorithm Choosing parameters Sensitivity to scaling Sensitivity to outliers Difficulty evaluating clusters without labels

metadata.section: 23. Important Limitations

text: A practical clustering workflow looks like: Raw Data ↓ Data Cleaning ↓ Feature Selection ↓ Feature Scaling ↓ Choose Clustering Algorithm ↓ Train Clustering Model ↓ Evaluate Clusters ↓ Visualize Clusters ↓ Interpret Clusters ↓ Use Clusters for Business/ML Decisions

metadata.section: 24. Complete Clustering Workflow

text: Clustering is an unsupervised learning technique used to discover hidden groups in data. The major algorithms include: K-Means ↓ Centroid-based clustering Hierarchical Clustering ↓ Tree/hierarchy of clusters DBSCAN ↓ Density-based clustering GMM ↓ Probabilistic clustering The most important idea is: Clustering does not learn predefined labels. It discovers structure in unlabeled data based on similarity, distance, density, or probability.
